title: Marriage without consent
subtitle: Forced marriage protection orders and the criminal offence under s 121 ASBCPA 2014
objectives: State the statutory definition of 'force' for forced marriage protection order purposes, and identify who may apply for an order
State the elements of the criminal offence of forced marriage under s 121 Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014
Explain clearly why forced marriage and arranged marriage are legally and factually distinct practices, and why conflating them is both a legal and a factual error

leadingAuthorities.role: Inserted Part 4A into the Family Law Act 1996, creating the forced marriage protection order

leadingAuthorities.citation: Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, s 121
leadingAuthorities.role: Creates the criminal offence of forcing a person to marry in England and Wales

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson sits next to a common misconception, and it's worth naming directly: forced marriage is not a feature of any one culture, religion or community — it is coercion, and it occurs across all of them, just as arranged marriage, a lawful and entirely different practice built on consent, also occurs across all of them. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You can name the statute — this lesson checks whether you can apply the legal test for force precisely, without leaning on assumptions about who is or isn't affected.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on scenario questions that test whether you can identify coercion (or its absence) from facts alone — not from any assumption about the people involved.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the forced/arranged distinction in mind throughout — it is the single most exam-relevant idea in this lesson, and every later part assumes you have it firmly fixed.

overview.hook: Two people are getting married with their families' active involvement in choosing the match. In one case, either party could have said no at any point and the marriage would not have gone ahead. In the other, one party has been told, in various ways, that saying no is not an option. The first is an arranged marriage — a long-standing, lawful practice found across many communities and religions, built entirely on the couple's own consent. The second is a forced marriage — a form of abuse, and since 2014 a criminal offence, regardless of who is involved or why. This lesson is about the law that separates the two, and about being precise where precision protects people rather than stereotypes them.

parts.heading: The distinction the law depends on getting right
parts.voice: structural — states the core distinction before any doctrine, because the doctrine only makes sense once it's fixed
body: Before any statute or case law, this lesson needs one distinction held firmly: forced marriage and arranged marriage are not points on a spectrum, and they are not the same practice under different names. An arranged marriage is one in which families or a wider community play an active role in introducing or proposing a match, but the decision to marry — and the ongoing freedom to say no, at any stage, including at the ceremony itself — remains entirely with the two people marrying. It is a lawful, widely practised tradition across many communities, religions and countries, entirely compatible with English law's requirement of free consent to marry.

A forced marriage is one entered into without the free and full consent of one or both parties, where some form of physical, emotional, financial or psychological pressure, coercion, deception, or abuse of a position of trust is used to bring the marriage about, or to prevent a person leaving it. The defining feature is not who arranged the introduction — it is whether genuine, freely given consent was present when the marriage took place.

It is important to be precise about who this affects, because misconceptions here cause real harm. Forced marriage is not a phenomenon confined to any one culture, faith, nationality or community — cases have been identified across a wide range of backgrounds, including among people with no minority ethnic or religious background at all. Treating it as a problem belonging to a particular community both stigmatises that community unfairly and risks blinding professionals to cases outside it. The law's focus, correctly, is on the presence or absence of consent and coercion in a given case — not on who the people involved are.

components.definition: A marriage entered into without the free and full consent of one or both parties, brought about or maintained by coercion, threats, deception, or other pressure. Distinct from arranged marriage, which is lawful and depends entirely on the free consent of both parties at every stage. Forced marriage occurs across all communities and is not attributable to any single culture or religion.

interaction.prompt: Is an arranged marriage, where families introduce the couple but both parties freely consent and could refuse at any stage, unlawful under English law?
options: No — arranged marriage is a lawful practice, entirely distinct from forced marriage, which turns on the presence of coercion
Yes — any marriage involving family involvement in choosing the match is treated as forced
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The law's concern is consent, not who was involved in the introduction. An arranged marriage with genuine, freely given consent at every stage is lawful and unremarkable in law.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what actually triggers legal intervention: coercion and absence of consent, not family involvement in proposing a match. Arranged marriage, properly understood, is a lawful practice resting entirely on both parties' free consent.

parts.heading: Defining 'force': the statutory test
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: The Forced Marriage (Civil Protection) Act 2007 inserted a new Part 4A into the Family Law Act 1996, creating the forced marriage protection order (FMPO) — a bespoke civil remedy designed specifically for this problem, sitting alongside (and in practice often working with) the non-molestation and occupation orders covered in the previous lesson.

The Act defines 'force' broadly and precisely, because forced marriage coercion is frequently psychological rather than physical, and the drafting needs to capture that reality. Force includes coercing by threats or other psychological means, and — a provision worth knowing precisely — it also includes knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent to marriage or to understand the nature of the marriage. This second limb matters because some victims are not being threatened in any conventional sense at all: they may have a learning disability, cognitive impairment, or other condition that means they cannot meaningfully consent, and someone is proceeding with the marriage regardless.

An FMPO can be made to protect a person from being forced into a marriage, or from any attempt to force them into one, and can equally protect someone already in a marriage they were forced into. The order's terms are flexible by design — the court can prohibit, restrict or require virtually any conduct necessary for the person's protection, including surrendering a passport, disclosing a person's whereabouts, or stopping specific individuals from contacting them.

components.citation: Family Law Act 1996, s 63A(4)–(6) (inserted by the Forced Marriage (Civil Protection) Act 2007)
components.text: For the purposes of this Part a person ('A') forces another person ('B') to enter into a marriage if A does anything for the purpose of causing B to enter into the marriage without B's free and full consent. 'Force' includes coerce by threats or other psychological means, and references to being forced to enter into a marriage are to be read accordingly. For the purposes of this Part, a person ('A') also forces a person ('B') to enter into a marriage if A purports to marry B where B lacks the capacity to consent to the marriage.
elements: Causing another person to enter into marriage without their free and full consent
'Force' includes coercion by threats or other psychological means, not only physical force
Knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent or to understand the nature of marriage also counts as forcing them into it

interaction.prompt: Under s 63A FLA 1996, does 'force' require physical violence or the threat of it?
options: No — it expressly includes coercion by psychological means, and also knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent
Yes — the statute requires an actual or threatened physical act
No, but only economic pressure counts alongside physical force
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The definition is deliberately broad — psychological coercion is expressly included, and so is proceeding with a marriage where a person lacks the capacity to consent at all, even absent any threat.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Read the definition again — it's not limited to physical force at all. Threats or other psychological means are expressly included, and so is knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent or understand the marriage.

parts.heading: Getting an order: who can apply, and how fast
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, walking through the process
body: One of the FMPO scheme's most distinctive features is how wide the pool of potential applicants is, because forced marriage victims are often unable — through fear, isolation, or practical restriction — to bring proceedings themselves. The person to be protected can apply directly, but so can a 'relevant third party' specified by the court (in practice, most commonly a local authority), and any other person can apply with the court's permission, which the court grants having regard to that person's connection with the protected person and their knowledge of the circumstances.

Because forced marriage cases often involve urgent risk — a planned trip abroad, an imminent ceremony, a passport about to be confiscated — the court can make an order without notice to the respondent where it is just and convenient to do so, with a return hearing at which the respondent can be heard. This ex parte route exists precisely because notifying a respondent in advance in a genuinely urgent case can itself increase the danger to the person the order is meant to protect.

Breach of an FMPO is a criminal offence in its own right (inserted by the same 2014 Act discussed in Part 4), which gives the civil order real enforcement force — exactly the same structural design as the non-molestation order in the previous lesson, where a civil protective order is backed by a standalone criminal sanction for breaching it.

components.label: Applying for a forced marriage protection order
points: The person to be protected can apply directly
A 'relevant third party' specified by the court (commonly a local authority) can apply without needing the court's separate permission
Any other person can apply with the court's permission, having regard to their connection to the protected person and knowledge of the circumstances
An order can be made without notice (ex parte) in urgent cases, with a return hearing to follow
Breach of an FMPO is itself a criminal offence, giving the civil order direct enforcement teeth

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order they would occur in a genuinely urgent forced marriage protection order application.
items: A local authority becomes aware a young person is at imminent risk of being taken abroad for a forced marriage
The local authority, as a relevant third party, applies to the court for a forced marriage protection order without notice to the family
The court makes an interim order without notice, given the urgency and risk of increased danger if notice were given
A return hearing is listed at which the respondent can be heard before any final order is made
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence urgency demands: risk identified, third-party application, an immediate without-notice order to protect against imminent harm, then a return hearing so the respondent's side is still heard before anything final.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — the without-notice order comes first, precisely because of the urgency and risk of alerting the respondent in advance; the respondent's opportunity to be heard comes afterwards, at the return hearing, not before the protective order is made.

parts.heading: When protection becomes prosecution: the criminal offence
parts.voice: direct — sets out the offence precisely, because precision protects people here
body: Since 2014, forcing someone to marry has been a standalone criminal offence in England and Wales, created by s 121 Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014. Before this, prosecutors had to rely on a patchwork of other offences — kidnapping, false imprisonment, assault — none of which named the wrong for what it was. Section 121 fixes that gap directly.

The offence is committed by a person who uses violence, threats, or any other form of coercion for the purpose of causing another person to marry, where the person using the coercion believes, or ought reasonably to believe, that the conduct may cause the other person to marry without free and full consent. A separate limb of the offence covers practising any form of deception with the intention of causing a person to leave the United Kingdom, where the purpose is to force that person into marriage — a provision aimed squarely at cases where a victim is misled into travelling abroad (for example, told it is a family holiday) as the mechanism for the forced marriage itself.

The offence carries a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment. Its civil and criminal siblings are designed to work together rather than in competition: a person seeking safety can pursue an FMPO for immediate protection without needing to trigger a criminal investigation at all, while a prosecution can proceed independently where the evidential and public interest tests for a criminal charge are met — mirroring exactly the civil/criminal parallel-track relationship covered in the previous lesson on domestic abuse.

components.citation: Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, s 121
components.text: A person commits an offence under the law of England and Wales if he or she — (a) uses violence, threats or any other form of coercion for the purpose of causing another person to marry, and (b) believes, or ought reasonably to believe, that the conduct may cause the other person to marry without free and full consent. A person commits an offence under the law of England and Wales if he or she practises any form of deception with the intention of causing another person to leave the United Kingdom, and intends the other person to be subjected to conduct outside the United Kingdom that is an offence under subsection (1) or would be an offence under subsection (1) if the victim were in England or Wales.
elements: Violence, threats or any other form of coercion
Used for the purpose of causing another person to marry
The defendant believes, or ought reasonably to believe, this may cause marriage without free and full consent
A separate limb: deception intended to cause a person to leave the UK, where the purpose is a forced marriage abroad

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly engages the deception limb of the s 121 offence, as distinct from the general coercion limb.
interaction.scenarioText: A father repeatedly threatens his daughter with violence unless she agrees to marry a man she has never met. When she continues to refuse, he tells her they are going on a two-week family holiday abroad, when in fact he intends for the marriage ceremony to take place there, out of reach of any protection she might seek in England.
tappableSpans: repeatedly threatens his daughter with violence
tells her they are going on a two-week family holiday
intends for the marriage ceremony to take place there
interaction.correctSpan: tells her they are going on a two-week family holiday
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the deception element — misleading her about the true purpose of the trip in order to get her out of the UK for a forced marriage abroad is precisely what the second limb of s 121 was drafted to capture, distinct from the threats already covered by the first limb.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the point where deception, rather than direct threats, is used to get her abroad — the threats already engage the first limb of s 121, but the second limb specifically targets being misled about the purpose of leaving the UK.

parts.heading: Holding the line: coercion is the test, not community
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by restating and reinforcing the core distinction
body: It's worth returning, at the close of this lesson, to where it began. The legal test for forced marriage — whether under the FMPO scheme or the s 121 offence — asks one question: was there coercion, deception, or an inability to consent, such that free and full consent was absent? It does not ask, and should never be treated by a student, a practitioner, or a court as asking, which community, religion, or nationality the people involved belong to.

This matters for two connected reasons. First, framing forced marriage as belonging to a particular culture is simply inaccurate — documented cases span an extremely wide range of backgrounds, and treating it as culturally specific risks both unfairly stigmatising communities where the overwhelming majority of marriages are entered into freely, including the vast majority of arranged marriages, and overlooking victims outside whatever group is stereotypically assumed to be at risk. Second, and just as importantly, conflating forced marriage with arranged marriage as practices — treating any family involvement in choosing a match as inherently suspect — risks pathologising a lawful, valued tradition and can make victims of genuine coercion less likely to come forward, precisely because they fear their whole community, and a legitimate tradition within it, will be blamed for one person's wrongdoing.

A well-constructed exam answer in this area does the same work this lesson has done: it identifies the legal test precisely, applies it to the facts given without importing assumptions the facts don't support, and states plainly, where relevant, that arranged marriage is a separate and lawful practice. That precision is not a stylistic nicety — it is the substance of getting this area of law right.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students sometimes answer a forced marriage problem question by inferring coercion from the ethnic, religious or national background of the people in the scenario, rather than from the facts describing what was actually said or done to the applicant.
components.whyItsWrong: The statutory tests under both the FMPO scheme and s 121 turn entirely on conduct — threats, coercion, deception, or incapacity to consent — never on the identity of the people involved. An answer that reasons from background rather than facts both mischaracterises the law and reproduces exactly the stereotyping the law's neutral drafting is designed to avoid.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario describes a forced marriage engaging these statutory protections, rather than a lawful arranged marriage?
interaction.scenarioA: A woman's parents introduce her to a family friend's son; she meets him several times over the following year, decides she likes him, and freely agrees to marry him, knowing she could have said no at any point.
interaction.scenarioB: A man's parents tell him he will marry a woman he has never met within the month, and make clear that refusing will mean losing all contact with his family and financial support, leaving him feeling he has no real choice.
interaction.explanation: B shows coercion — pressure calculated to remove any genuine choice, engaging both the FMPO scheme and potentially the s 121 offence. A is a properly consensual arranged marriage: family involvement in the introduction, but free and full consent throughout, which the law does not touch.

testPool.prompt: Name the Act that created the forced marriage protection order.
testPool.modelAnswer: The Forced Marriage (Civil Protection) Act 2007, which inserted Part 4A into the Family Law Act 1996.

testPool.prompt: Name the provision that created the criminal offence of forcing a person to marry in England and Wales, and its maximum sentence.
acceptableAnswers: s 121 Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, seven years
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 121 Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, carrying a maximum sentence of seven years' imprisonment.

testPool.prompt: Under s 63A FLA 1996, is a marriage 'forced' only where physical violence is used?
options: No — psychological coercion, threats, and knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent are all expressly included
Yes — the statute requires physical violence or its direct threat

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is the most accurate statement about who may apply for a forced marriage protection order?
options: The protected person, a relevant third party (such as a local authority), or another person with the court's permission
Only the person to be protected can apply — third parties have no standing
Only a local authority can apply, and never the protected person directly
testPool.trapExplanation: Both wrong options describe an artificially narrow applicant pool. The scheme is deliberately broad precisely because victims are often unable to bring proceedings themselves — third parties and, with permission, other connected individuals can apply too.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best explains why an arranged marriage does not, on its own, engage the forced marriage protection framework?
options: Because the statutory test turns on whether free and full consent was present, and family involvement in proposing a match does not, by itself, remove consent
Because arranged marriages are legally presumed to be non-consensual unless proven otherwise
Because the framework only applies to marriages taking place outside the United Kingdom
testPool.trapExplanation: The wrong options both misstate the law in ways that would wrongly sweep in a lawful practice or wrongly narrow the framework's geographic reach. The test is, and only ever is, whether coercion removed free and full consent — not where the marriage occurs, and not a presumption against any particular form of introduction.

testPool.prompt: In the extract from s 63A FLA 1996 below, highlight the clause covering a person who cannot consent because of incapacity, as opposed to a person who is coerced.
testPool.passage: For the purposes of this Part a person ('A') forces another person ('B') to enter into a marriage if A does anything for the purpose of causing B to enter into the marriage without B's free and full consent. 'Force' includes coerce by threats or other psychological means. For the purposes of this Part, a person ('A') also forces a person ('B') to enter into a marriage if A purports to marry B where B lacks the capacity to consent to the marriage.
testPool.ratioSentence: a person ('A') also forces a person ('B') to enter into a marriage if A purports to marry B where B lacks the capacity to consent to the marriage

testPool.prompt: In the extract from s 121 ASBCPA 2014 below, highlight the phrase describing the required mental element as to the victim's consent.
testPool.passage: A person commits an offence under the law of England and Wales if he or she uses violence, threats or any other form of coercion for the purpose of causing another person to marry, and believes, or ought reasonably to believe, that the conduct may cause the other person to marry without free and full consent.
testPool.ratioSentence: believes, or ought reasonably to believe, that the conduct may cause the other person to marry without free and full consent

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that forced marriage, as a matter of documented fact, is confined to any single culture, religion or nationality?
sliderLabels: Confident it is confined to a specific community
Confident it cuts across all communities
testPool.correctPosition: Confident it cuts across all communities
testPool.explanation: Cases of forced marriage have been documented across a very wide range of backgrounds, including among people with no minority ethnic or religious background. Treating it as confined to any one community is factually inaccurate and legally irrelevant to the statutory test.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that arranged marriage, where both parties freely consent throughout, is itself unlawful in England and Wales?
testPool.explanation: Arranged marriage with genuine, freely given consent is a lawful and long-standing practice. Nothing in the FMPO scheme or the s 121 offence touches it — both are triggered by coercion and absence of consent, not by how the couple were introduced.

testPool.prompt: A 19-year-old with a significant learning disability, who does not have the capacity to understand what marriage involves, is taken through a marriage ceremony by relatives who know of her condition. No threats are made and she does not resist. Does this fall within the statutory definition of a forced marriage?
options: Yes — knowingly taking advantage of her incapacity to consent to, or understand, the marriage is itself defined as forcing her into it
No — since no threats were made and she did not resist, there is no coercion and therefore no forced marriage
No — capacity is irrelevant to the statutory definition
testPool.explanation: Section 63A's second limb covers exactly this: proceeding with a marriage while knowingly taking advantage of a person's incapacity to consent counts as forcing them into it, entirely independently of whether any threat was made or resistance shown.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is most likely to satisfy the s 121 offence's deception limb specifically?
testPool.scenarioA: A woman is told directly and repeatedly that she will be disowned if she does not marry the man her family has chosen, and eventually agrees under that pressure while still in the UK.
testPool.scenarioB: A woman is told she is going on a short family trip abroad; only once there does she discover the true purpose was to force her into a marriage arranged without her knowledge.
testPool.explanation: B is the deception limb precisely: being misled about the purpose of leaving the UK in order to bring about a forced marriage abroad. A is coercion within the UK, engaging the general coercion limb of s 121 or an FMPO instead, but not the deception-to-leave-the-UK limb specifically.

testPool.prompt: A young man's parents have introduced him to a woman they hope he will marry, and have made clear they would be pleased if the match went ahead. He has met her twice, likes her, and has told his parents he is considering it but has not yet decided. Analyse whether this engages the forced marriage protection framework.
factsToOrder: His parents introduced him to the prospective match
They have expressed a hope the marriage will go ahead
He has met her twice and reports liking her
He has told them he is still considering it and has not committed

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether these facts show a forced marriage engaging Part 4A FLA 1996 or the s 121 offence, or a lawful arranged marriage outside their scope.
modelAnswer.rule: A marriage is 'forced' under s 63A FLA 1996 where a person acts for the purpose of causing another to marry without free and full consent, including by coercion, threats or psychological pressure, or by knowingly taking advantage of an incapacity to consent. Family involvement in proposing a match, without more, does not meet this test.
modelAnswer.application: The facts show parental involvement in the introduction and an expressed hope, but no threats, pressure, or removal of choice — he remains free to decide, has met her willingly, and has not yet committed. There is no indication of coercion, deception, or incapacity of any kind.
modelAnswer.conclusion: This is a properly consensual arranged marriage in progress, not a forced marriage. Neither the FMPO scheme nor the s 121 offence is engaged on these facts, and no legal intervention is warranted or appropriate.

testPool.prompt: What is the legal consequence of breaching a forced marriage protection order?
options: Breach of an FMPO is itself a criminal offence, giving the civil order direct enforcement force
Breach carries no sanction beyond a fresh application for the same order
Breach can only be addressed through separate civil contempt proceedings, never as a criminal matter

testPool.prompt: A concerned teacher believes a student is at risk of being forced into marriage abroad during the summer holidays. The student's family is not aware the teacher has any suspicions. What is the most accurate description of the teacher's options?
options: The teacher, or more likely a local authority alerted by the teacher, can apply for a forced marriage protection order, including without notice to the family in a genuinely urgent case
The teacher has no standing to raise the matter at all, since only the student herself can apply
An order can only be sought once the student has already been taken abroad
testPool.explanation: The applicant pool is deliberately wide, including third parties such as local authorities (often prompted by exactly this kind of professional concern), and orders can be made without notice, and in advance of any actual removal, precisely to prevent harm before it occurs.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is letting assumptions about culture or community stand in for the actual legal test. The statutory question is always whether coercion, deception or incapacity removed free and full consent — never who the people involved are, and never whether family members were involved in proposing the match at all.
